text: The argument runs between a grandfather and a grandson, and its subject is horses. Caballito criollo, made in Argentina in 1953, hands a young breeder a theory about how the animals and the trade around them might be brought into a changed era, and hands the older man every reason to distrust it. Ralph Pappier takes a hundred minutes over the disagreement, which is long enough for it to stop being a debate and start being a way of sharing a house. Ranch pictures usually run on weather and prices. This one runs on the slower fact that the person who must be convinced is family, and that proof, where animals are concerned, takes seasons rather than arguments. It carried the Silver Condor for Best Film.

Opera is expensive, formal, and easy to damage, which is what makes it ideal material for men with no stake in keeping it intact. The Marx Brothers work their way through contracts, staterooms and the boxes of a great house, nominally to get two singers onto a stage together, actually to spoil an evening for everyone who paid for it. Ninety-one minutes, and Sam Wood never lets a scene settle into decorum long enough to become respectable. The aim is precise: not the music, which the film performs straight, but the people who own the seats and the manners that come with them. It sits on the National Film Registry. The plot is there to be interrupted, and the interruptions escalate — first the language, then the furniture, then the architecture of the occasion itself.

A schoolmaster walks into a cabaret to catch his pupils out, and is still there long after they have gone. Germany, 1930: Josef von Sternberg gives Immanuel Rath a classroom in which everything is fixed — the hour, the seat, the deference owed him — and then a room where none of it applies. Chalk, timetable and a place at the front all have an opposite inside the club. Lola Lola's work is to be wanted by men who pay to sit near her, and Rath's error is to assume that a wedding removes the audience. The film is interested less in appetite than in the speed of the exchange. A hundred and eight minutes, and the standing that made him legible to himself was never his own property. It was lent by the school, and Der blaue Engel is unhurried about collecting on the loan.

Some of it was arranged for the camera, and that is the first fact about the film rather than the last. Robert Flaherty's 1922 picture follows Inuit families in northern Quebec through the ordinary work of not dying in cold: raising a shelter out of the ground's own material, taking food from water and ice, moving when the season says move. Seventy-nine minutes without dialogue, and the camera keeps to process — how a thing is made, from start to finish, in the order it is made. The arrangement of the scenes belongs to the filmmaker. The competence in front of the lens does not. That is where the charge is: what has been staged and what has merely been recorded occupy the same frame, and the film offers no help in telling them apart.

Two boys finish high school in a Texas town that is running out of reasons to exist. Sonny is sleeping with the coach's wife, Duane has the girl everybody else wants, and graduation keeps approaching with no plan behind it that survives contact with the place. Peter Bogdanovich lays out the options plainly: the army, a business somebody else got tired of running, or staying. A hundred and nineteen minutes of small decisions that turn out to be permanent. What gives the film its weight is that the adults are no further along than the boys — the same affairs, the same waiting, one generation deeper in — so the escape being contemplated has already been declined by everyone within driving distance. Nothing is punished or rewarded in any orderly way.

A girl who is beaten at home and a Chinese Buddhist with no standing in the city cross paths in a London the film treats as merciless. D.W. Griffith gives them eighty-nine minutes, and the tenderness between them is assembled out of very small acts — a shelf set straight, a length of cloth, a face that stops bracing for the next blow. The scale is the surprise: one street, two rooms, three people, in 1919. The title carries the vocabulary of the period that made it, and that vocabulary is inside the picture as well as on the poster; watching it now means holding the delicacy and the condescension at the same time. What survives is the quiet — kindness offered in a place where none is expected.

Once a year, 130 million workers set out for home at the same time. Lixin Fan puts a camera inside that number and keeps it on a single family: parents who work far from the village their family lives in, a journey made annually and at cost, a few days of reunion asked to carry twelve months of absence. Eighty-five minutes, and the difficulty turns out to be domestic rather than logistical. The stations supply the scale — bodies against barriers, waiting measured in days — but the film makes its case indoors, at close range, where wages sent back have not bought the closeness they were meant to buy. China's rise is the weather here, not the subject. The subject is what one household spends to be part of it.

Rural southern Illinois, and a reunion that had gone a decade without happening. In 1995 Steve James drove back to find Stevie Fielding, a troubled boy he had been paired with through an advocacy program and then left behind; the return is the premise, and the camera he brings is immediately part of what is under examination, because a man arriving with equipment is not the same as a man arriving. A hundred and forty-five minutes is long for a documentary, and the length is the method — the film stays well past the point where a shorter one would have delivered its verdict. What accumulates is a question the director cannot ask from behind the lens without also answering it: what was owed here, by whom, and when it stopped being paid.

A door in the apartment stays locked, and the film treats it as the shortest route into a century of Serbian politics. Mila Turajlić films her mother in Belgrade, and the flat does the structural work: family history and national history arrive through the same rooms, by the same hallway, which is the film's economy and also its argument. A hundred and four minutes, largely indoors, largely two people talking. The Lux Prize went to it. Films about political inheritance usually head for archives and newsreel; this one mostly stays home, and lets a mother's account and a sealed doorway carry what footage would carry elsewhere. That the interviewer is the daughter changes every question, and the film leaves the change in rather than editing around it.

A camera followed André Hazes for months and did not confine itself to the stage. John Appel's portrait takes in the concerts and then the business meetings, the house, the family, a holiday in Benidorm — the places where a film about a popular singer either turns into publicity or stops being one. Eighty-six minutes, and the register shifts without notice between the comic and the wounded, sometimes within one scene. Folk singing of this kind runs on plain feeling delivered on demand, and what Appel keeps returning to is the cost of supplying it at home as well as on a bill. The warmth is real and it is also the work. The film is at its best when both of those are in the room at once.

Filed as a documentary and also as a comedy, and neither label lasts long. Gert de Graaff nests one story inside another and then inside a third, and builds the seams out of optical tricks: a hundred minutes of a picture quietly rearranging what it has already shown. The mechanism is the subject — there is no separate story hiding behind the apparatus, only the apparatus, examined. It took the European Film Award for European Discovery of the Year. The pleasure runs closer to a puzzle box than to an essay: each layer is cut so that the one above it has to be reconsidered, and the reconsidering is the event. Where it ends up is a proposition about the person in the seat, arrived at by construction rather than assertion.
